analysis.one_liner: Imposes a one-time 14.25% tax on wealth above $10 million to pay down the national debt.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in April 2017 and never received a vote, dying when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a one-time tax of 14.25% on the portion of any American's or trust's net worth above $10 million, excluding the value of a primary home and its mortgage [S2, S3]. It was deliberately framed around President Trump's own 1999 proposal for a similar wealth tax, citing his statement that it would raise $5.7 trillion and pay off the national debt [S3]. The revenue would go toward reducing the federal debt, which the bill's findings argue benefits future generations and the broader economy [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: All taxpayers share in the intended benefit: a smaller national debt means less federal money spent on interest and less burden passed to future generations, per the bill's own findings [S3]. The tax itself falls only on households and trusts with net worth above $10 million [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Applies only to net worth above $10 million, leaving the vast majority of households untouched [S2, S3].
Excludes the value of a family's principal residence and the mortgage debt on it, so homeowners' primary asset is not counted [S3].

The bill's findings estimate that if the tax raised the $5.7 trillion Trump projected for his 1999 plan, it would cover all war-on-terror spending obligations and cut the debt-to-GDP ratio from 77% to 46% [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and trusts with net worth over $10 million would owe a one-time tax of 14.25% on everything above the $10 million threshold, valued as of the date the law took effect under estate-tax-style valuation rules [S3]. That is a small, extremely wealthy slice of the population.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households and trusts worth over $10 million

drawbacks.text: The tax is one-time only: it taxes existing wealth once, as of the enactment date, and does nothing about the ongoing deficits that push the debt back up afterward [S3].
Valuing every asset a multimillionaire or complex trust holds on a single date, using estate-tax rules, would be an enormous administrative challenge and invites disputes over appraisals [S3].
The bill does not dedicate its revenue to any specific purpose, so Congress could redirect it rather than using it for debt reduction as the findings suggest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A large, one-time transfer from the very wealthiest households toward the public balance sheet, with the main honest objections being its one-time nature (deficits would resume) and the difficulty of valuing wealth accurately. The bill was also openly political: it used the President's own 1999 statements to challenge his party to support it, which helps explain why it drew only one cosponsor and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Juan Vargas introduced the bill on April 25, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1, S5].
One Democratic member cosponsored it; no further action was ever taken [S4, S5].
The bill's findings section quotes Donald Trump's 1999 description of his own wealth tax plan and argues that enacting it would fulfill his promise and substantially reduce the national debt [S3].
The bill died at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019, without a committee vote or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households and trusts with net worth above $10 million are better off, since the one-time 14.25% levy never took effect; the national debt continued to grow as it otherwise would have [S5, S3].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy households; the debt burden remained

for.name: Rep. Juan Vargas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means, framing it around President Trump's own 1999 wealth tax proposal

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Kevin Brady, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or a vote

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill and one Democrat cosponsored it; with Republicans controlling the House and the Ways and Means Committee, the bill never advanced, and no Republican support is recorded [S4, S5].

industries.industry: Households and trusts with net worth above $10 million
industries.note: The bill would tax everything they own above $10 million at 14.25%, one time. Avoiding the tax keeps that wealth intact, while the public forgoes the debt reduction the revenue could have funded [S3].

industries.industry: Wealth management and tax advisory firms
industries.note: A one-time wealth levy of this size would have generated large restructuring and valuation work for estates and trusts, work that disappears when the bill dies. Its stake is modest compared with their clients' direct tax exposure.
